It's been overwhelmingly negative recently, but here's some perspective on how supply-constrained demand from $LITE to $MU looks amid possible AI capex slowdowns. 

As one Korean executive on memory puts it: 

"Thirty people are already lined up at a restaurant that is full, and five of them leaving does not create a table."

The amount of tables might expand, but supply shortages and price hikes in bottlenecks can persist through capex slowdowns or capacity buildout. 

From AI implications in medicine, physics, materials, robotics, cybersecurity, engineering, energy, to AI itself over the next 5-10 years... 

We've only reached the precipice of the next technological paradigm shift. 

The world is going to need a lot more compute.

text:
You didn't get a dumber Claude this month. You got old prompts.

Half the rules you wrote were for a model that no longer exists, and they are quietly breaking the new one.

An Anthropic engineer posted a 3-minute fix last night. 4,400 people saved it. Most of them don't know it works outside Claude Code too. Here's the command, and the one-prompt version for everyone else.

The command: /doctor prompt-audit, inside Claude Code (version 2.1.283 or newer). It reads your CLAUDE.md, skills, agents and custom commands and flags the lines written for older models: ALL CAPS emphasis, step-by-step babysitting, workarounds the new model does not need, paths and commands that no longer exist, two files that contradict each other. You get the file and line, the quote, the reason, a confidence level and a proposed fix. It changes nothing without your yes. About 3 minutes. Add a folder after the command to narrow it.

Peter Yang's reply under the post: so useful it should run on its own.

Why this matters outside Claude Code: your Projects instructions, your custom GPT, the 400-word system prompt you paste every morning. All written for a model you don't use anymore. Here is the same audit as a prompt:

Prompt: Prompt audit
"Here are my saved instructions for [Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini], written over the last year: [paste]. I now use [model]. Go line by line. For each line give me a table: the line, what problem it was solving, whether [model] still needs it (yes / no / unclear), the risk of keeping it (contradiction, outdated, empty emphasis, wasted tokens), and the replacement. Then write the new version at most 70% of the original length, keeping every rule that still matters. Finish with the 3 rules for [model] that I am missing and most people add."

Run it once per model release. Four times a year, 10 minutes each.

Most "the model got dumber" complaints are old prompts meeting a new model.

More prompts you can run today in the God of Prompt library. 7,200+ prompts, free, no signup. Link in the first reply.

When did you last reread your own Claude instructions?
